The Second Punic War. From 218 to 201 BCE, Rome and Carthage fought a titanic struggle for dominion over the Mediterranean. It began when Hannibal, Carthage's brilliant general, crossed the Alps with roughly 26,000 soldiers and African war elephants, bringing the war to Italy itself and shocking Rome with this audacious invasion. Hannibal then won a series of stunning victories. At the Trebia River in 218 BCE, at Lake Trasimene in 217 BCE, and most infamously at Cannae in 216 BCE. At Cannae, his tactical double envelopment perfectly annihilated a Roman army of 80,000 soldiers, one of the worst defeats in Roman history. Yet Rome refused to surrender. Instead, Rome responded by abandoning pitched battles and adopting a strategy of attrition and harassment under Fabius Maximus, earning him the epithet "the Delayer" for his cautious approach. The war devastated Italy for years as Hannibal marauded the countryside, but Rome controlled the seas and maintained supply lines and reinforcements from home. Then Scipio Africanus emerged as Rome's answer to Hannibal. A brilliant young general, Scipio trained new armies and invaded Carthage's North African homeland to draw Hannibal back. Scipio defeated Hannibal decisively at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE, forcing Carthage to surrender, pay a massive indemnity, and surrender its Mediterranean territories. The war ended Carthaginian power and left Rome the undisputed dominant power over the Mediterranean for the next two centuries, reshaping the ancient world's balance of power.
